podcast.title: Detrimental Managerial Contract with David Bowie
podcast.body: From the early 1970s, Tony DeFrees had a "terrible arrangement" as David Bowie's manager, which left Bowie financially "skint" despite his numerous platinum albums and chart-topping singles. Although Bowie left DeFrees in 1975, the contract allowed DeFrees to continue collecting royalties on Bowie's records until 1996. "Seeing the early 70s, he entered a terrible arrangement with manager Tony DeFrees, and even with all the platinum albums and chart-topping singles, he was close to Skint, he had nothing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Managerial Support for Bowie's Image (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: Tony DeFries became David Bowie's manager in the late 1970s and was highly supportive of Bowie's innovative artistic endeavors, including his experimental approach to rock music and his decision to wear a dress in public. "And he was only too happy to help Bowie search for a new approach to rock music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Manager Tony DeFries' Early Guidance (1970-1972)
xref.body: Tony DeFries, a solicitor by profession, signed on as Bowie's manager in 1970 when Bowie was a struggling young singer. Within approximately 18 months, DeFries secured Bowie a new deal with RCA records and proceeded to transform him into an international star. The entirety of Bowie's early 1970s career, including the iconic Ziggy Stardust era, was carefully guided by DeFries.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Contractual Dispute with Main Man (1972-1975)
xref.body: David Bowie wanted out of his contract with Tony DeFries' management company, Main Man, by the end of 1974, just two years into their relationship. Despite selling millions of albums, Bowie realized that most of the profits were not reaching him, suspecting that the new contract signed with Main Man at the end of September 1972 was "weird." On January 29, 1975, Bowie informed RCA, his record label, of his intention to split from DeFries, sparking a battle over who owned Bowie's next album.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bitter Split from Tony DeFries (April 1975)
xref.body: Following Bowie's decision to split from Tony DeFries, a 48-hour marathon negotiation took place in April 1975 to finalize his departure. The terms of the split were so harsh that it's said Bowie broke down and cried at the conference table, remaining in shock for a week. The agreement stipulated that Bowie could leave only if Main Man took half of his earnings from albums dating back to *Hunky Dory* in 1971 through an upcoming live album, and DeFries was guaranteed 16% of Bowie's gross earnings for the next seven years, through to 1982.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bowie Bonds (1997) – Financial Innovation
xref.body: In 1997, Bowie collaborated with New York investment banker David Pullman to create "Bowie Bonds," a package of securities backed by the future projected royalties of 25 Bowie albums (287 songs recorded before 1990). Bowie received $55 million upfront, using the money to buy back rights he had lost to his former manager. This was a pioneering use of intellectual property to secure a financial instrument. "In 1997, a New York investment banker named David Pullman put together a package of securities backed by the future projected royalties of 25 Bowie albums, a total of 287 songs that were recorded before 1990."

xref.title: Manager Tony DeFries
xref.body: Bowie's new manager, Tony DeFries, believed that for Bowie to succeed, he needed a provocative image and a weird brand marketed alongside his music. DeFries encouraged Bowie to experiment with makeup and costumes, a plan Bowie embraced. He acquired long, flowing, and expensive gowns from a designer named Mr. Fish, continuing a tendency to dress to shock that dated back to his mod days in high school. "DeFries encouraged Bowie to experiment with makeup and costumes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Manager Tony DeFries (Late 1970s)
xref.body: In the late 1970s, David Bowie acquired Tony DeFries as his manager, who actively supported Bowie's search for new artistic approaches to rock music, including his decision to wear a dress in public. "In the late 1970s, he acquired a new manager, a character by the name of Tony DeFries."
